text.p: CardioGenesis Corp on Monday said it had started a clinical trial with a minimally invasive technique for a procedure that uses lasers to shoot tiny holes in the heart to improve blood supply to areas blocked by plaque or fatty deposits.

In a statement released during the American Heart Association's annual scientific sessions here, CardioGenesis said two patients suffering from angina due to severe coronary artery disease were treated last week in Germany.
They were treated with the company's Percutaneous Myocardial Revascularization, or PMR, system.
The first patient has been released from the hospital and the other is expected to be released this week.

CardioGenesis said it was the first company to start human clinical trials with the minimally invasive technique. The laser treatment had been used before, but after the cutting of an incision to expose the beating heart.

But with the PMR system, the patient remains conscious and the beating heart is accessed through a small puncture in the upper thigh. A CardioGenesis guiding and steering catheter system is then placed into the femoral artery, passed across the aortic valve and positioned within the left ventricle.
The system is is designed to be used by interventional cardiologists in a cardiac catheterization laboratory, as opposed to treatments performed by surgeons in an operating room, CardioGenesis said.
The company cautioned it was too early to draw any conclusions as to the success of the first procedures.

CardioGenesis said its initial clinical studies of the PMR System will be conducted at teaching institutions in Europe. It plans to apply to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for permission to start U.S. human clinical trials of the PMR system in the first half of 1997.
